Project 01

SLIDEX

A fully automated kinetic LED totem system featuring 5 independent Totems, each capable of 3 Degrees of Freedom — vertical movement, rotation, and horizontal sliding — all orchestrated over Ethernet and ESP‑NOW wireless communication.

5Totems
4LED Cabinets / Totem
3Degrees of Freedom
25Slave ESP32s
5Master ESP32s
01 System Architecture Overview

Per Totem Structure

  • 4 × LED Cabinets (stacked vertically)
  • 1 × IHSS86-80 Sliding Motor (bottom)
  • 1 × Master ESP32 with Ethernet
  • 4 × Slave ESP32 (one per cabinet)
  • 3 Degrees of Freedom per Totem

Per Cabinet Structure

  • 1 × NEMA Stepper — Vertical movement
  • 1 × IHSS36-30 — Rotation via RS485
  • 1 × Slave ESP32 (controller)
  • Cabinet 4 = Slave_4_5 (also controls slider)
  • Step/Dir driver for NEMA motor

Communication Stack

  • Ethernet — PC → Master ESP32
  • ESP-NOW — Master → Slave (unicast)
  • RS485 Modbus RTU — Slave → IHSS motors
  • Step/Dir — Slave → NEMA driver

Degree of Freedom Summary

  • ↕ Vertical — NEMA Stepper, Step/Dir
  • ↻ Rotation — IHSS36-30, RS485
  • ↔ Horizontal Slide — IHSS86-80, RS485

↻ Rotation IHSS36-30 RS485 Modbus RTU Cabinet ESP32 (Slave 1–4)
↔ Horizontal Sliding IHSS86-80 RS485 Modbus RTU Bottom ESP32 (Slave_4_5)

RS485 (Stepper Motor)

Each cabinet is a self-contained control unit. The Slave ESP32 manages two motors independently: the NEMA stepper motor for vertical travel via Step/Dir pulses through a dedicated motor driver, and the IHSS36-30 servo for rotation via RS485 Modbus RTU through a MAX485 transceiver chip.

A 24V DC power supply feeds the motor drivers directly and steps down to 5V via a buck converter to power the ESP32 logic. The bottom cabinet (Slave_4_5) contains an additional RS485 channel to control the IHSS86-80 horizontal sliding motor mounted beneath the totem.

03 Total System Wiring Diagram
Full 5-Totem System — Network & Signal Architecture
Ethernet (PC → Master)
ESP-NOW (Master → Slaves)
RS485 → IHSS86-80 Slider
Slave_4_5 (Special)

All 5 Totems connect to a central LAN Hub via Ethernet cable. The PC running the show-control software sends structured commands to each Totem's Master ESP32 independently over the local network.

Each Master routes commands internally via ESP-NOW unicast — a Wi-Fi peer-to-peer protocol — only to its own 4 slave cabinets. Masters never cross-communicate with other Totems' cabinets, keeping the control boundaries clean and deterministic.

The Slave_4_5 in each Totem is a dual-purpose controller: it manages Cabinet 4's rotation motor (IHSS36-30) AND the bottom sliding motor (IHSS86-80), both via RS485 Modbus RTU on the same bus.

04 Code Flow Diagram
Firmware Execution Flow — PC → Master ESP32 (UDP) → Slave ESP32 (ESP-NOW) → Motor
UDP — PC to Master (192.168.1.4:8888)
ESP-NOW — Master to Slave (Unicast)
RS485 Modbus RTU → IHSS Motor
Step/Dir Pulses → NEMA Motor
General Commands (local execution)

The PC sends structured command strings via UDP to the Master ESP32 at 192.168.1.4 : 8888. The Master listens continuously with udp.parsePacket() and reads the incoming string into a buffer.

The Master parses the string using strtok() to split on commas, extracting the command type, motor ID, target position, and speed. General commands (like MTCHK, DEBUG,ON, SET,MAC) are handled locally on the Master. Motor commands (NEMA / MOVE) are forwarded.

For motor commands, the Master looks up the target Slave's MAC address from the motor ID, packs the data into a struct, and fires esp_now_send() as a unicast Wi-Fi peer packet. The Slave's OnDataRecv() callback fires instantly. It verifies the motor ID matches, then branches: NEMA triggers step/dir pulse generation for vertical movement; MOVE writes a Modbus RTU frame over RS485 to the IHSS servo for rotation or horizontal sliding.

07 Slidex Application — GUI Overview

The Slidex App is a custom Windows desktop application that serves as the primary control interface for the entire SLIDEX system. It sends all UDP commands directly to the Master ESP32 at 192.168.1.4 : 8888. The app is organised into tabs: Slidex App (the main control panel), Scenario 1–10 (pre-programmed timed sequences), and Config (OSC video trigger setup).

Screen 1 — Main Control Panel (Slidex App Tab)
Slidex App — Main Tab

🟦 Totem Motor Selection Grid

  • 5 Totem columns — each Totem has its own panel
  • Each Totem shows: Top Second Third Fourth cabinet rows + Sliding
  • Each cabinet row has 2 checkboxes: the left one selects the IHSS servo (MOVE), the right selects the NEMA stepper
  • The bottom Sliding row = IHSS86-80 horizontal slider for that Totem
  • 🔴 Red indicator = motor is offline / not responding
  • Select All / Deselect All buttons per Totem for batch selection
  • Top-right: Select All Motors / Deselect All Motors across all 5 Totems

🟦 Position & Speed Controls

  • POSITION input — target position value for selected motors
  • SPEED input — movement speed for selected motors
  • SEND POSITION — sends MOVE,n,position,speed or NEMA,n,position,speed to each checked motor. Nothing sends until at least one motor is checked
  • JOG +/JOG − — incremental movement by configured step amount (default 10)
  • Top input box = custom command field (free-type any UDP command)

🟦 Action Buttons

  • EMERGENCY STOP — sends ESTOP,n,0,0 to all checked motors immediately
  • REFRESH CONNECTION — re-establishes UDP socket and pings all motors
  • ZERO MOTOR — sends ZERO,n or ZERON,n to set current position as home
  • ALARM RESET — sends ALMRST,n to clear motor alarms
  • LOOSEN BRAKES — sends LNBRK,n to release motor brakes
  • STOP MOTOR — sends STOP,n using configured deceleration

🟦 Network Config & Output

  • IP field — Master ESP32 IP address (default: 192.168.1.255 broadcast)
  • Ports field — listening ports for UDP responses
  • SET — applies new IP/port settings
  • GET — reads back current network config
  • Black console panel (bottom right) — displays all outgoing & incoming UDP traffic in real time
  • Clear All — clears the console output

🟦 Scenario & Video Playback

  • S1 input — scenario number to play (1–10)
  • PLAY SCENARIOS — executes the selected scenario tab's command list
  • Loop checkbox — loops the scenario continuously
  • RC: 4000 — response delay/timeout in milliseconds
  • V1 input + PLAY VIDEOS — triggers OSC video playback configured in the Config tab

🟦 How Motor ID Mapping Works

  • Each Totem has 5 motor rows. Motor IDs increment across Totems:
  • Totem 1: IHSS IDs 1–4 (cabinets), sliding = ID 5
  • Totem 2: IHSS IDs 6–9, sliding = ID 10
  • NEMA motors have their own separate ID numbering
  • Checking left checkbox of a row → MOVE,n command
  • Checking right (NEMA) checkbox → NEMA,n command

Screen 2 — Scenario Editor (Scenario Tab)
Slidex App — Scenario 1 Tab

📋 What is a Scenario?

  • A scenario is a plain-text list of UDP commands executed sequentially
  • Each line = one UDP command + an optional time delay appended as the last value
  • The delay is in seconds and tells the app how long to wait before sending the next line
  • Up to 10 independent scenarios (tabs: Scenario 1–10), each saveable separately
  • Scenarios can be triggered from the main tab using the PLAY SCENARIOS button

📋 Scenario Line Format

  • Standard motor command: MOVE,1,5000,50,5
  • The last number 5 = wait 5 seconds after sending before proceeding
  • If delay is 0 — command fires immediately, no wait
  • NEMA example: NEMA,2,10000,100,3 — moves NEMA 2 then waits 3 s
  • The delay value is stripped before sending — only MOVE,1,5000,50 is transmitted over UDP

📋 Reading the Scenario List

  • NEMA,1,100000,100,0 — NEMA 1 to 100k steps, no wait
  • NEMA,21,100000,100,1 — NEMA 21, then wait 1 s
  • MOVE,5,-21000,50,0 — IHSS motor 5 to -21000
  • MOVE,25,21000,50,4 — IHSS motor 25, wait 4 s
  • NEMA,24,-100000,100,12 — wait 12 s after this move
  • Mix of NEMA and MOVE commands creates choreographed multi-totem motion

📋 Scenario Playback Controls

  • Click the Scenario 1 (or any) tab to open that scenario's command list
  • Edit commands directly in the text area
  • Save button (bottom) — persists the scenario to disk
  • From the main tab: type scenario number in S1 field → press PLAY SCENARIOS
  • Enable Loop to repeat the scenario endlessly
  • RC value (e.g. 4000 ms) = global response timeout between commands if no delay is specified

Config Tab (OSC Video Playback): The app also includes a Config tab where each action button or motor event can be mapped to an OSC (Open Sound Control) message. This allows the SLIDEX system to trigger external media servers or video playback software (such as Resolume or QLab) in sync with motor movements. The video number is entered in the V1 field on the main panel, and PLAY VIDEOS fires the configured OSC message to the media server over the network.

Quick Reference — GUI Workflow

Check the IHSS or NEMA checkbox next to the cabinet/sliding row in the desired Totem panel
② Enter Position & Speed
Type target position and speed values in the POSITION and SPEED input fields
③ Send Command
Press SEND POSITION — the app sends MOVE,n,pos,spd or NEMA,n,pos,spd via UDP to the Master
④ Monitor Output
Watch the black console panel for sent commands and motor feedback responses in real time

Project 02

Curtain Facade

The Curtain Facade is a kinetic installation of 15 independent Totems, each containing one IHSS36-30 RC servo motor that physically opens and closes a curtain panel. The system is centrally commanded by a Controllino industrial PLC which listens for simple UDP commands from the Application PC and broadcasts RS485 motor commands simultaneously to all 15 motors.

01 System Architecture & Wiring
Curtain Facade — Full System Wiring Diagram

🖶 Application PC

  • Sends OPEN or CLOSE UDP commands over Ethernet
  • Targets Controllino at 10.0.0.4 : 8001
  • No direct motor knowledge — only high-level intent commands
  • Receives status feedback responses on port 8888

⚙️ Controllino (PLC Controller)

  • Industrial Arduino-compatible PLC with native Ethernet
  • IP: 10.0.0.4 — listens on UDP port 8001
  • Parses UDP commands and builds RS485 motor instructions
  • Sends to motor ID 0x00 — the RS485 broadcast address that commands ALL devices on the bus simultaneously
  • Outputs RS485 to the LAN Splitter

🔀 LAN Splitter (RS485 Signal Splitter)

  • Not a standard Ethernet hub — this is a dedicated RS485 signal repeater/fan-out device
  • Takes the single RS485 line from the Controllino and distributes it to all 15 Totems
  • Ensures signal integrity and prevents reflections from daisy-chaining
  • All 15 motors receive the identical command at the same instant

🔧 15× IHSS36-30 RC Motors (Totems)

  • Each Totem contains one IHSS36-30 closed-loop servo motor
  • All motors respond to RS485 broadcast address 0x00
  • Connected in parallel via RS485 from the LAN Splitter outputs
  • All 15 curtains open or close in perfect synchronisation
  • On startup: auto-homed and brakes released before accepting commands

04 Firmware Code
C++ / Controllino 
// Curtain Facade - Controllino UDP to RS485 Motor Controller
// IP: 10.0.0.4  Listen: UDP 8001  Reply: UDP 8888
// 15 Totems, 1x IHSS36-30 each. ID 0x00 = RS485 broadcast (all motors)

#include "Arduino.h"
#include <Controllino.h>
#include <Ethernet.h>
#include <EthernetUdp.h>
#include "RCmotor.h"

byte mac[] = { 0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE, 0xEF, 0xFE, 0xEE };
IPAddress controllino_ip(10, 0, 0, 4);
const uint16_t ListeningPort = 8001;
const uint16_t SendingPort   = 8888;
char packetBuffer[UDP_TX_PACKET_MAX_SIZE];
EthernetUDP Udp;

// 16 motor slots (ID 0x00 = broadcast, IDs 0x01-0x0F = individual Totems)
const int NUM_MOTORS = 16;
RCMotor motors[NUM_MOTORS] = {
    RCMotor(0x00), RCMotor(0x01), RCMotor(0x02), RCMotor(0x03),
    RCMotor(0x04), RCMotor(0x05), RCMotor(0x06), RCMotor(0x07),
    RCMotor(0x08), RCMotor(0x09), RCMotor(0x0A), RCMotor(0x0B),
    RCMotor(0x0C), RCMotor(0x0D), RCMotor(0x0E), RCMotor(0x0F)
};

float ACCELERATION = 3.0, DECELERATION = 3.0;
bool  emergencyStop = false;
String command; long id, degrees, speed, timeS;

bool parseCommand(const String& data) {
    char buf[255], cmd[10];
    data.toCharArray(buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (sscanf(buf, "%[^,],%ld,%ld,%ld", cmd, &id, &degrees, &speed) >= 1) {
        command = String(cmd); return true;
    }
    return false;
}

void sendToAll(const String& msg) {
    Udp.beginPacket(Udp.remoteIP(), SendingPort);
    Udp.print(msg); Udp.endPacket();
}

void handleCommand() {
    int m = (int)id;

    // Primary facade commands
    if (command == "OPEN") {
        // motors[0] = RS485 address 0x00 = broadcast to ALL 15 Totems
        motors[0].Rotate(2000, 30);
    }
    else if (command == "CLOSE") {
        // Return all curtains to home position (0 steps)
        motors[0].Rotate(0, 30);
    }
    // Direct motor commands (individual or broadcast via ID)
    else if (command == "MOVE")   { motors[m].Rotate(degrees, speed); }
    else if (command == "ESTOP")  { motors[m].MotorEmergencyStop(); emergencyStop = true; }
    else if (command == "ERESUME"){ motors[m].MotorStart(); emergencyStop = false; }
    else if (command == "STOP")   { motors[m].MotorStop(); }
    else if (command == "ZERO")   { motors[m].Zero_motor(); }
    else if (command == "LNBRK")  { motors[m].LoosenBrake(); }
    else if (command == "ALMRST") { motors[m].AlarmReset(); }
    else if (command == "PING")   { sendToAll("PONG"); }
    else if (command == "MTCHK") {
        for (int i = 1; i < NUM_MOTORS; i++) {
            sendToAll(String(i) + "," + (motors[i].MotorCheck() ? "ON" : "OFF"));
            delay(10);
        }
    }
    else if (command == "SETAD")  { motors[m].Setup((float)degrees, (float)speed); }
    else                              { sendToAll("ERROR: Unknown command"); }
}

void setup() {
    Ethernet.begin(mac, controllino_ip); delay(1000);
    Udp.begin(ListeningPort);
    Serial.begin(115200); delay(1000);
    // Initialise all motor slots: configure -> home -> release brake
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_MOTORS; i++) {
        motors[i].Setup(ACCELERATION, DECELERATION); delay(10);
        motors[i].Home_motor_method2(0); delay(10);
        motors[i].LoosenBrake(); delay(500);
    }
    Serial.println("Curtain Facade ready. Listening on port 8001");
}

void loop() {
    if (Udp.parsePacket()) {
        Udp.read(packetBuffer, UDP_TX_PACKET_MAX_SIZE);
        Serial.print("RX: "); Serial.println(packetBuffer);
        if (parseCommand(String(packetBuffer))) handleCommand();
        memset(packetBuffer, 0, sizeof(packetBuffer));
    }
}
05 System Explanation

The Curtain Facade achieves full synchronisation of 15 curtain motors through a single RS485 broadcast. The key design decision is using motor ID 0x00 — the Modbus broadcast address — which instructs every RS485 device on the bus to respond simultaneously without needing individual addressing.

The Controllino is an industrial Arduino-compatible PLC chosen for its native Ethernet, robust power handling, and reliable RS485 output. The Application PC only ever sends OPEN or CLOSE. All motor-level details (step count, speed, RS485 framing) are completely abstracted inside the firmware. OPEN internally maps to motors[0].Rotate(2000, 30) and CLOSE maps to motors[0].Rotate(0, 30) — since motors[0] has RS485 address 0x00, both calls broadcast to all 15 Totems at once.

The LAN Splitter — critically not a standard Ethernet hub — is a dedicated RS485 signal repeater and fan-out device. It receives the single RS485 output from the Controllino and distributes it across all 15 motor connections with proper signal conditioning, preventing reflections and degradation that would occur from daisy-chaining. All 15 Totems receive the command at effectively the same instant.

On startup, the firmware runs a full motor initialisation loop: every motor slot is configured with acceleration/deceleration parameters, homed to its zero reference via Home_motor_method2(), then its brake is released with a 500 ms settling delay. This guarantees a known, consistent mechanical state before any operational command is accepted.

Project 03

Tic-Tac-Toe — Human vs Robot

An interactive physical Tic-Tac-Toe installation where a human player places RFID-tagged pucks on a 3×3 board, and a robotic arm plays as the opponent. The system ties together 9 Arduino RFID readers, a Controllino PLC (10 relays for LEDs + electromagnet), a Game PC running an AI algorithm, and an industrial robot controlled via Modbus TCP — all networked through a central LAN hub.

01 System Architecture & Wiring
Tic-Tac-Toe — Full System Wiring Diagram

🎮 9× Arduino + RFID Readers

  • Each board position has a dedicated Arduino with RFID reader
  • Human places an RFID-tagged puck (disguised as X or O) on a position
  • Arduino detects the tag and sends N,ON (e.g. 1,ON) via UDP to the Game PC
  • All 9 Arduinos connect to the Game PC through the LAN Hub
  • Game PC listens on UDP port 8888 for incoming RFID events

⚙️ Controllino (Relay + Electromagnet)

  • Controls Relays R1–R9 — each relay powers the LED light under one board position
  • Controls Relay R0 (R10) — activates/deactivates the Electromagnet on the robot arm
  • IP: 192.168.1.10 — listens on UDP port 8001
  • Receives commands like R1 ON, R0 OFF from the Game PC
  • R0 (electromagnet) also has automatic I16 hardware input for safety

💻 Game PC (AI + Coordinator)

  • Runs main.py — a PySide6 GUI with the Tic-Tac-Toe AI
  • Listens for RFID UDP events from Arduinos on port 8888
  • Sends relay commands to Controllino via UDP port 8001
  • Sends robot movement commands to Robot Controller via Modbus TCP port 502
  • AI difficulty selectable: Easy / Medium / Hard (minimax-style algorithm)
  • Connects via LAN Hub to all devices

🤖 Robot Controller

  • Industrial robot arm that physically places O pucks on the board
  • Communicates via Ethernet / Modbus TCP to the Game PC
  • IP: 192.168.1.200 — Modbus port 502
  • Has pre-programmed movements for all 9 board positions plus home position
  • Picks puck using Electromagnet (R0) — Game PC toggles magnet ON to grab, OFF to release
  • Game PC triggers moves via Modbus coil writes (address range 533+)

02 Complete Game Flow
① HUMAN PLACES PUCK
Human places RFID puck on position N. Arduino at position N detects tag and sends N,ON via UDP to Game PC (port 8888)
② GUI UPDATES
Game PC receives N,ON, marks position N as X on the GUI board, and immediately sends RN ON to Controllino to light the LED under that position
③ LED LIGHTS UP
Controllino receives RN ON, closes relay N, illuminating the LED under position N on the physical board to confirm the human's move
④ AI COMPUTES MOVE
Game PC AI evaluates the board (Easy/Medium/Hard difficulty) and determines the best position for O. GUI shows "Robot moving..."
⑤ MAGNET ON → PICK PUCK
Game PC sends R0 ON to Controllino to activate the electromagnet. Game PC then sends Modbus coil write to robot to perform the pick movement
⑥ ROBOT MOVES TO POSITION
Game PC sends Modbus coil write to address 533+N (toggle ON then OFF) to command the robot arm to move to board position N and place the O puck
⑦ MAGNET OFF → RELEASE
Game PC sends R0 OFF to Controllino to deactivate the electromagnet, releasing the puck at the chosen position. Game PC also sends RN ON to light that position's LED
⑧ TURN RETURNS TO HUMAN
GUI updates O position, checks for win/tie. If game continues, GUI shows "Your move..." and waits for the next RFID puck placement. Win/tie triggers LED blink animation across winning positions

05 Controllino Firmware
C++ / Controllino 
// Tic-Tac-Toe - Controllino Relay + Electromagnet Controller
// IP: 192.168.1.10  Listen: UDP 8001
// R0 = Electromagnet (auto via I16 or manual)
// R1-R9 = LED position lights for 3x3 board

#include <Controllino.h>
#include <Ethernet.h>
#include <EthernetUdp.h>

byte mac[] = { 0x50, 0xD7, 0x53, 0x00, 0xC5, 0x66 };
IPAddress ip(192, 168, 1, 10);
unsigned int localPort = 8001;
EthernetUDP Udp;

int relayPins[10] = {
  CONTROLLINO_R0, CONTROLLINO_R1, CONTROLLINO_R2, CONTROLLINO_R3, CONTROLLINO_R4,
  CONTROLLINO_R5, CONTROLLINO_R6, CONTROLLINO_R7, CONTROLLINO_R8, CONTROLLINO_R9
};
// R0 = electromagnet, R1-R9 = board position LEDs

bool manualR0Control = false;
bool relayStates[10] = {false};

void setup() {
  Ethernet.begin(mac, ip);
  Udp.begin(localPort);
  Serial.begin(115200);
  for (int i = 0; i <= 9; i++) {
    pinMode(relayPins[i], OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(relayPins[i], LOW);
  }
  pinMode(CONTROLLINO_I16, INPUT);
  // I16 hardware input: LOW = magnet OFF, HIGH = magnet ON (auto mode)
}

void loop() {
  handleElectromagnetControl();  // Auto R0 via I16 when not in manual mode
  int sz = Udp.parsePacket();
  if (sz) {
    char buf[255];
    int len = Udp.read(buf, 255);
    if (len > 0) buf[len] = 0;
    String cmd = String(buf);
    cmd.trim(); cmd.toUpperCase();
    processUDPCommand(cmd);
  }
}

void handleElectromagnetControl() {
  if (manualR0Control) return;  // Manual override active — skip auto
  int state = digitalRead(CONTROLLINO_I16);
  digitalWrite(relayPins[0], state == LOW ? LOW : HIGH);
  relayStates[0] = (state != LOW);
}

void processUDPCommand(String cmd) {
  if (cmd == "RESET") {
    for (int i = 0; i <= 9; i++) digitalWrite(relayPins[i], LOW);
    manualR0Control = false; return;
  }
  if (cmd == "AUTO")   { manualR0Control = false; return; }
  if (cmd == "STATUS") { printStatus(); return; }

  // Parse "RN ON" or "RN OFF"
  int sp = cmd.indexOf(' ');
  if (sp > 0) {
    String relay  = cmd.substring(0, sp);
    String action = cmd.substring(sp + 1);
    if (relay.startsWith("R") && (action == "ON" || action == "OFF")) {
      int n = relay.substring(1).toInt();
      if (n >= 0 && n <= 9) {
        bool on = (action == "ON");
        digitalWrite(relayPins[n], on ? HIGH : LOW);
        relayStates[n] = on;
        if (n == 0) manualR0Control = true; // Switch R0 to manual
      }
    }
  }
}
06 System Explanation

The Tic-Tac-Toe installation creates a seamless physical-digital feedback loop. When the human places a puck, the RFID Arduino at that position detects the tag and fires a N,ON UDP packet to the Game PC. The PC simultaneously updates the GUI and sends a relay command to the Controllino to illuminate the LED under that square — giving the human immediate physical confirmation of their move.

The Controllino manages two categories of outputs: Relays R1–R9 control the individual LED position lights under each board square (one per position), while Relay R0 controls the electromagnet mounted on the robot arm. R0 has a dual-mode design — it operates automatically via the hardware I16 input during normal robot operation, but the Game PC can override it manually with R0 ON/OFF commands when it needs precise control over the pick-and-release sequence.

The robot sequence on each computer turn begins with the Game PC sending a Modbus TCP coil write to address 528 + D to trigger the pick movement (D is a counter that cycles 0–4 to select different pick motions). After a settling delay, the PC sends coil 533 + N to move the arm to the chosen board position, where it releases the puck by deactivating the electromagnet.

The AI algorithm in main.py uses a minimax-style strategy on Hard difficulty: first checking if it can win immediately, then blocking any immediate human win, then preferring the center, then corners, then any available space. On win or tie, the winning position LEDs blink three times via rapid R1–R9 OFF/ON UDP sequences to the Controllino, providing a satisfying physical light animation on the board itself.

The game script is located at HANDOVER\TIC-TAC-TOE\main.py. Network settings (IP addresses, ports, AI difficulty) are stored in config.ini in the same directory and can be adjusted via the in-app settings panel without restarting.

C++ / Arduino
// ESP_CODE_ANALOG.ino — Marker firmware (Tiny Pico ESP32)
// Reads analog pin 32 to detect charging pod placement.
// Broadcasts status via ESP-NOW and controls NeoPixel LED ring.

#include <Arduino.h>
#include <Adafruit_NeoPixel.h>
#include <esp_now.h>
#include <WiFi.h>
#include <Preferences.h>

#define LED_PIN        19
#define LED_COUNT      16
#define SENSOR_PIN     32
#define SENSOR_THRESHOLD 1500

// Broadcast to Master ESP32 via ESP-NOW
uint8_t broadcastAddress[] = {0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF};

Adafruit_NeoPixel strip(LED_COUNT, LED_PIN, NEO_RGB + NEO_KHZ800);
Preferences preferences;

// Startup color loaded from non-volatile memory
int brightness, redVal, greenVal, blueVal;
bool lastSensorState = false;

void setup() {
  strip.begin();
  preferences.begin("led-config", false);
  redVal     = preferences.getInt("startR", 200);
  greenVal   = preferences.getInt("startG", 100);
  blueVal    = preferences.getInt("startB", 0);
  brightness = preferences.getInt("brightness", 255);
  strip.setBrightness(brightness);
  updateStatic();

  // Read initial sensor state to avoid false trigger on boot
  lastSensorState = (analogRead(SENSOR_PIN) > SENSOR_THRESHOLD);

  WiFi.mode(WIFI_STA);
  esp_now_init();
  // Register send/receive callbacks and broadcast peer...
}

void loop() {
  // Analog edge detection with debounce
  bool current = (analogRead(SENSOR_PIN) > SENSOR_THRESHOLD);
  if (current != lastSensorState) {
    delay(50);
    if ((analogRead(SENSOR_PIN) > SENSOR_THRESHOLD) == current) {
      lastSensorState = current;
      sendESPNowMessage(current ? "8,OFF" : "8,ON"); // number = marker ID
    }
  }
}

// Commands received via ESP-NOW from Master:
//   red / green / blue / white / off       → preset colors

//   brightness:40                           → set brightness 0-255
//   glow / train / stop                     → LED effects

// Bridges UDP (Ethernet via W5500) ↔ ESP-NOW.
// Receives marker status via ESP-NOW → broadcasts UDP on port 8001.
// Receives control commands via UDP on port 8005 → forwards to all markers via ESP-NOW.

// W5500 Ethernet module pins (SPI)

// UDP config

const uint16_t broadcastPort = 8001; // outgoing marker status to Unity

// ESP-NOW → UDP: marker status forwarded to Unity

  broadcastUDP(buf);
}

// UDP → ESP-NOW: control commands forwarded to all markers
void checkUDP() {
  // reads from port 8005 → sendESPNow(buf) → all markers receive simultaneously
}

Explanation

The DCT system is built around 9 wireless LED markers, each containing a Tiny Pico ESP32, a 16-pixel NeoPixel LED ring, a 3.7V LiPo battery with wireless charging, and a 5V booster to power the LEDs. The wireless receiver inside each marker picks up a signal from the charging pod; this signal passes through a voltage divider (20K + 30K resistors) to safely step the 5V output down to 3.3V before reaching the Tiny Pico's analog pin 32.

The firmware reads pin 32 continuously using edge detection with a 50ms debounce. When the analog value crosses the threshold of 1500, it means the marker has been placed in a pod — the Tiny Pico broadcasts N,OFF (where N is the marker number) via ESP-NOW. When it drops below threshold (marker lifted), it sends N,ON. Boot color, brightness, and effect settings are all loaded from non-volatile Preferences storage so markers remember their configuration across power cycles.

The Master ESP32 sits on the network at 192.168.1.120 with a W5500 Ethernet module connected over SPI. It acts as a pure bridge: status messages received from markers via ESP-NOW are immediately UDP-broadcast on port 8001 to the Unity application. In the opposite direction, control commands sent via UDP to port 8005 are forwarded via ESP-NOW broadcast to all 9 markers simultaneously.

The full set of control commands (sent UDP to 192.168.1.120:8005) is:

CommandExampleEffect
Preset colorred / green / blue / whiteSet all markers to named color
Custom RGB0,200,255Set all markers to custom RGB value
Brightnessbrightness:40Set LED brightness (0–255)
Glow effectglowSlow pulsing breathing effect
Train effecttrainAnimated wipe forward and back
Stop effectsstopReturn to static color
Store boot colormain red / main 0,200,50Save color to flash — survives power cycle
Turn offoffSet all LEDs to black

The main command writes the chosen color into the ESP32's NVS (non-volatile storage) and triggers a restart. From that point forward the marker boots into that color automatically, making it the permanent default until changed again.

Project 05

Projection Book

Project Overview

The Projection Book is an interactive bilingual installation built around a physical book whose 8 pages have been injected with RFID tags at precise locations. Nine RFID readers (8 for page detection + 1 for RFID 9) are positioned beneath or around the book stand so that flipping to any page brings its embedded tag into range of the corresponding reader.

Two Force Sensitive Resistors (FSRs) act as language selectors — one triggers English mode, the other Arabic mode. Once a language is selected, the system knows which bank of video clips to draw from in Resolume, and every subsequent page flip maps to the correct bilingual content automatically.

All hardware communicates over Ethernet via UDP to a central LAN hub. A Python middleware application (main_v4.py) running on the Resolume PC listens on UDP port 8000, interprets the incoming messages, and fires the appropriate OSC commands to Resolume on port 9000 to trigger the correct video clips.

RFID Reader Code (Arduino + PN532)

C++ / Arduino
/*************************************************************
 *  Projection Book – RFID Page Reader
 *  One Arduino + PN532 per reader station (9 total)
 *  Each unit monitors for a specific tag UID. When the tag
 *  enters range it sends N,ON; when it leaves, N,OFF.
 *************************************************************/
#include <Wire.h>
#include <SPI.h>
#include <Adafruit_PN532.h>
#include <Ethernet.h>
#include <EthernetUdp.h>

// ── Network Configuration ─────────────────────────────────
byte         mac[]       = { 0x3C, 0xE7, 0xF1, 0x08, 0x39, 0xE6 };
IPAddress   local_ip(192, 168, 1, 102);   // Change per unit
IPAddress   server_ip(192, 168, 1, 100);  // Resolume PC
unsigned int local_port  = 8002;
unsigned int server_port = 8001;         // PC listens here (forwarded to main_v4.py :8000)

// ── RFID Tag UID for this page (change per reader) ────────
String CODE1 = "1ddf7ff2";  // e.g. Page 2 tag UID

// ── PN532 (I²C via IRQ/RESET pins) ───────────────────────
#define PN532_IRQ    (2)
#define PN532_RESET  (3)
Adafruit_PN532 nfc(PN532_IRQ, PN532_RESET);
EthernetUDP Udp;

String code;
bool click1  = true;
bool endflag = true;

void setup() {
  delay(1000);
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Ethernet.begin(mac, local_ip);
  Udp.begin(local_port);
  nfc.begin();
  if (!nfc.getFirmwareVersion()) while (1); // Halt if PN532 not found
  nfc.SAMConfig();
  Serial.println("RFID Reader Ready");
}

void rfid_read() {
  code = "";
  uint8_t uid[] = { 0,0,0,0,0,0,0 };
  uint8_t uidLen;
  nfc.readPassiveTargetID(PN532_MIFARE_ISO14443A, uid, &uidLen, 100);
  code = String(uid[0], HEX) + String(uid[1], HEX)
       + String(uid[2], HEX) + String(uid[3], HEX);
}

void loop() {
  rfid_read();
  check_data();
}

void check_data() {
  if (code == CODE1) {
    // Tag in range — send ON once (rising edge)
    if (click1) {
      click1  = false;
      endflag = true;
      Udp.beginPacket(server_ip, server_port);
      Udp.print("2,ON");   // Change number per reader (1–8)
      Udp.endPacket();
    }
  } else {
    // Tag removed — send OFF once (falling edge)
    if (endflag) {
      delay(70);
      endflag = false;
      Udp.beginPacket(server_ip, server_port);
      Udp.print("2,OFF");  // Change number per reader (1–8)
      Udp.endPacket();
    }
    click1 = true;
  }
}

FSR Language Selector Code (Arduino + Ethernet)

C++ / Arduino
/*************************************************************
 *  Projection Book – FSR Language Selector
 *  Two FSR units: one sends ENG,1 (English), one sends AR,1 (Arabic)
 *  When pressure exceeds THRESHOLD it fires a one-shot UDP message.
 *  The message is only re-sent after pressure drops and rises again.
 *************************************************************/
#include <Ethernet.h>
#include <EthernetUdp.h>

// ── FSR Pin & Threshold ───────────────────────────────────
const int  fsrPin    = A2;
const int  THRESHOLD = 500;   // 0–1023; adjust for physical sensitivity
bool       thresholdExceeded = false;

// ── Network Configuration ─────────────────────────────────
byte      mac[]         = { 0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE, 0xEF, 0xFE, 0xED };
IPAddress ip(192, 168, 1, 177);
IPAddress broadcastIP(255, 255, 255, 255);
unsigned int udpPort = 8005;
EthernetUDP Udp;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Ethernet.begin(mac, ip);
  Udp.begin(udpPort);
  delay(1000);
  Serial.println("FSR Language Selector Ready");
}

void loop() {
  int fsrValue = analogRead(fsrPin);

  if (fsrValue >= THRESHOLD && !thresholdExceeded) {
    thresholdExceeded = true;
    sendMessage("ENG,1");  // Change to "AR,1" on the Arabic FSR unit
  } else if (fsrValue < THRESHOLD && thresholdExceeded) {
    thresholdExceeded = false;  // Ready for next press
  }
  delay(100);
}

void sendMessage(const char* message) {
  Udp.beginPacket(broadcastIP, udpPort);
  Udp.write(message);
  Udp.endPacket();
  Serial.println(message);
}

Python Middleware — main_v4.py

Python
import socket
from pythonosc import udp_client

# ── Network Config ────────────────────────────────────────
UDP_LISTEN_PORT  = 8000   # Receives messages from all RFID / FSR nodes
OSC_TARGET_IP    = "127.0.0.1"
OSC_TARGET_PORT  = 9000   # Sends OSC to Resolume (loopback)

layer         = 1           # All clips live on Layer 1
language_mode = "ENG"       # Default: English
last_command  = None        # Guards against rogue language switches

osc_client = udp_client.SimpleUDPClient(OSC_TARGET_IP, OSC_TARGET_PORT)

def send_osc_connect(clip_id):
    addr = f"/composition/layers/{layer}/clips/{clip_id}/connect"
    osc_client.send_message(addr, [])

def parse_message(msg):
    global language_mode, last_command
    msg = msg.strip()

    # ── Language selection (only accepted after 1,OFF or 8,ON) ──
    if msg in ("ENG,1", "AR,1"):
        if last_command in ("1,OFF", "8,ON"):
            language_mode = "ENG" if msg == "ENG,1" else "AR"
        return

    # ── Page commands (N,ON / N,OFF where N = 1–8) ──────────────
    if "," in msg:
        channel_str, state = msg.split(",")
        channel = int(channel_str)
        if not 1 <= channel <= 8: return
        last_command = msg

        if language_mode == "ENG":       # Clips 1–9
            clip_id = channel + 1 if state == "ON" else channel
        else:                             # AR — Clips 13–21, reversed
            rev = 9 - channel
            clip_id = rev + 12 if state == "ON" else rev + 13

        send_osc_connect(clip_id)

How It Works

Physical Book & RFID Tags: The book's 8 pages each have an RFID tag injected at a precise location within the page itself. Nine PN532 readers are mounted in the installation frame beneath the book, each aligned to a specific page position. When a page is flipped and laid flat, its embedded tag comes within range of its assigned reader (at least 60 mm clearance required for reliable detection).

Page ON / OFF Events: Each Arduino uses edge detection to fire only on state changes. The moment a tag enters range: N,ON is sent via UDP. The moment it leaves: N,OFF is sent (with a 70 ms debounce delay to avoid noise on removal). This ensures exactly one trigger per event with no repeated firing.

Language Selection via FSR: Before or after finishing the book, the viewer presses one of two physical FSR buttons. FSR 1 broadcasts ENG,1 (English clips 1–9) and FSR 2 broadcasts AR,1 (Arabic clips 13–21). The middleware only accepts a language change when the last page command was 1,OFF or 8,ON — i.e. the book is at its start or end — preventing accidental language switches mid-read.

Clip Mapping Algorithm: In English mode, an ON event maps to clip = channel + 1 (page opened) and an OFF maps to clip = channel (page lifted). In Arabic mode the channel is reversed (9 - channel) before the same offset is applied, mirroring the right-to-left reading order across clips 13–21.

Project 06

Cube & Sphere Touch

Project Overview

The goal of this project was to create a touch-sensitive LED surface on both a sphere and a cube. Rather than using conventional capacitive touch sensors, the solution leverages a DFRobot mmWave Radar sensor — a millimetre-wave radar that detects subtle changes within its field of view with high precision.

The key insight is that mmWave radar works most accurately when its radio waves are focused onto a specific point. To achieve this, a conductor plate is used as a waveguide, directing and concentrating the radar beam precisely to the area where a touch needs to register on the LED surface. By adjusting the distance between the waveguide and the detection zone, the sensitivity threshold can be fine-tuned for reliable, repeatable triggering.

When a presence (touch) is detected by the sensor, the system performs 3 consecutive confirmation checks to validate the reading and eliminate false positives. Once confirmed, an OSC message is sent over UDP via Ethernet to the Main PC, which uses it to trigger a video change on the sphere or cube display.

mmWave Waveguide Technique

🎯 The Problem

mmWave sensors emit a wide-angle radio beam. Without focusing, the detection zone is too broad and unreliable for precise touch detection on a small LED surface area.

✅ The Solution

A metallic conductor plate acts as a waveguide, channelling and focusing the radar beam onto the exact touch point. Distance from the sensor to the target can then be adjusted to tune sensitivity.

Wiring Diagram

From (Voltix ESP32)To (mmWave Sensor)Wire ColourNotes
Pin 17 (UART RX)TX■ GreenmmWave TX → ESP32 RX
Pin 16 (UART TX)RX■ BlueESP32 TX → mmWave RX
V (3.3V / 5V)V■ RedPower supply to sensor
GNDGND■ BlackCommon ground
Voltix ESP32 → Main PC via Ethernet (OSC/UDP on port 9000)

Code

C++ / ESP32 Arduino
// Cube & Sphere Touch — mmWave Radar Presence Detection
// Voltix ESP32 | DFRobot mmWave Sensor | OSC over UDP/Ethernet
#include <SPI.h>
#include <Ethernet.h>
#include <EthernetUdp.h>
#include <OSCMessage.h>
#include <DFRobot_mmWave_Radar.h>

// ── Network Config ──
byte mac[] = { 0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE, 0xEF, 0xFE, 0xED };
IPAddress ip(192,168,1,4);           // ESP32 static IP
IPAddress destIp(255,255,255,255);  // Broadcast to PC
unsigned int destPort = 9000;        // OSC destination port
unsigned int localPort = 8888;       // Local listening port
EthernetUDP Udp;

// ── mmWave Sensor — UART2 (GPIO16=TX, GPIO17=RX) ──
HardwareSerial mySerial(2);
DFRobot_mmWave_Radar sensor(&mySerial);

// ── Detection State ──
bool currentPresence = false, previousPresence = false;
int  consecutiveDetections = 0;
const int REQUIRED_CONSECUTIVE = 2;  // 2 back-to-back reads required
unsigned long detectionTime = 0;
bool waitingForInitialMessage = false;
const unsigned long DELAY_BEFORE_INITIAL = 1000;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Ethernet.begin(mac, ip); Udp.begin(localPort); delay(1000);
  mySerial.begin(115200, SERIAL_8N1, 17, 16);  // RX=17, TX=16
  sensor.factoryReset(); delay(500);
  sensor.DetRangeCfg(0, 5);    // Detect 0–500 cm
  sensor.OutputLatency(0, 0);  // Immediate response
  sendOSCMessage("/composition/layers/3/clips/3/connect"); // Boot state
}

void loop() {
  checkForReset();
  processRadarDetection();
}

void processRadarDetection() {
  int presence = sensor.readPresenceDetection();
  previousPresence = currentPresence;

  // Require N consecutive positive reads before confirming presence
  if (presence == 1) {
    if (consecutiveDetections < REQUIRED_CONSECUTIVE) consecutiveDetections++;
  } else {
    consecutiveDetections = 0;  // Reset on any missed reading
  }
  currentPresence = (consecutiveDetections >= REQUIRED_CONSECUTIVE);

  // Rising edge: absence → presence
  if (currentPresence && !previousPresence) {
    sendOSCMessage("/composition/layers/3/clips/5/connect"); // Trigger video
    detectionTime = millis(); waitingForInitialMessage = true;
  }
  // Falling edge: presence → absence
  else if (!currentPresence && previousPresence) {
    waitingForInitialMessage = false;
  }
}

void sendOSCMessage(const char* address) {
  OSCMessage msg(address);
  Udp.beginPacket(destIp, destPort);
  msg.send(Udp); Udp.endPacket(); msg.empty();
}

void checkForReset() {
  if (Udp.parsePacket()) {
    char buf[255]; int len = Udp.read(buf, 255);
    if (len > 0) buf[len] = 0;
    if (strcmp(buf, "RESET") == 0) ESP.restart();
  }
}

How It Works

Detection & Confirmation: The mmWave sensor continuously scans its detection zone. Each positive reading increments a consecutive-detection counter. Only when 2 back-to-back readings confirm presence does the system register a touch — eliminating noise and single-frame false positives.

OSC over UDP: On a confirmed rising edge (absent → present), the ESP32 immediately broadcasts an OSC message over UDP on port 9000 to the Main PC. The OSC address path specifies which video clip to activate on the sphere or cube (e.g. /composition/layers/3/clips/5/connect). No message is sent on release — only the touch trigger matters.

Waveguide Focus: The conductor plate mounted in front of the sensor acts as a physical waveguide, narrowing and directing the radar beam to the precise surface area designated as the touch zone. This makes detection both highly localised and immune to ambient movement outside the target area.

Emergency Reset: The system also listens on UDP port 8888. Sending the string RESET remotely reboots the ESP32 via ESP.restart(), allowing recovery without physical access.

Signal Flow
mmWave Sensor
Detects presence
→
ESP32 (Voltix)
Validates ×2 reads
→
OSC / UDP
Port 9000 → PC
→
Main PC
Triggers video clip
